Key bugs: parse_u64 sets out=0 first, violating "out unchanged on failure" (e.g. "12x" leaves out=0 instead of caller's value; also overflow wraps silently, e.g. "18446744073789595916" wraps, no rejection above UINT64_MAX). Also empty string accepted (returns true with out=0) — contract says nonempty only. Also parse_u64 marked noexcept but fine.

Registry: get returns string_view into vector's string; concurrent add may push_back causing reallocation/remove of elements — but strings themselves: push_back moves strings; reallocation moves string objects but the character buffers? std::string's internal buffer may be allocated on stack/heap; moving a std::string copies ownership — the data pointer inside the string object moves with the object (string_view refers to the character data owned by the string, which lives in heap or in the moved object?). Actually string_view refers to the character data owned by the string, which lives in heap (or in the moved object during move construction — move ctor steals pointer, so data pointer stays valid). But if vector reallocation happens while reader holds view, the string objects move; move construction transfers the pointer, so the heap buffer stays. However small strings may be stack-allocated (C++17: "moved" strings? no—C++17 requires move ctor to leave source valid but spec says data may be stack allocated; move ctor can copy stack buffer). If source string's buffer is inside the vector's storage (stack allocated), moving to new vector storage copies the buffer into the new location; old location still holds a copy? Move ctor leaves source in valid but unspecified state — it may have transferred pointer, leaving source empty. If buffer was stack-allocated inside vector element storage, and vector reallocates, the old element storage is freed... Actually vector reallocation: allocates new array, move-constructs elements into new array, then dealloc_block destroys old elements and frees old array. If move ctor copied stack buffer into new array, source's buffer is in old array which gets destroyed — but the moved-to new array holds its own copy, fine. But if move ctor transferred pointer (heap), fine too. The dangerous case: reader holds string_view referring to buffer inside old vector element storage; then add triggers reallocation; move ctor may leave source's buffer... C++17 move ctor: "the move constructor is declared... the values of the source string are transferred; the source is in valid but unspecified state". If buffer is stack-allocated, move ctor must copy the buffer to destination; source's buffer remains in old storage until old storage destroyed — but reader's view points to old storage buffer which is destroyed after move. Hmm, but reader's view was obtained before reallocation; the view points into old element's buffer. During reallocation, old element is move-constructed into new array; then old array destroyed. If move ctor transferred pointer (heap case), view still valid. If stack case, view pointed to old storage which gets destroyed → dangling. So get returning view while add pushes → potential dangling. Also names[i] with no bounds check — get(i) out of range is UB, but contract doesn't mention; still a defect: no bounds validation. Also get returns view while holding lock then releases; concurrent add may push_back causing reallocation — that's the main memory bug. Also names.push_back(std::move(s)) while another thread holds view: same as above.

Also parse_u64 overflow: out*10 wraps, returns true for values > UINT64_MAX (e.g. "18446744073789595916" wraps to some value, returns true) — contract violation: must reject. Also empty string: returns true, contract says nonempty only. Also out=0 on failure: contract says out unchanged on failure — violation. Also parse_u64 marked noexcept but fine.
